claims.text: Adding a low volume fraction of well-dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles to a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its radiation tolerance.
The Y2O3 addition will not degrade the alloy's mechanical strength.
The Y2O3 addition will preserve processing feasibility.
Approximately 1–2 wt% fine Y2O3 nanoparticles can be incorporated uniformly through powder metallurgy.
Nanoscale Y2O3 particles create additional defect sinks in the alloy microstructure.
The additional defect sinks promote recombination of irradiation-induced point defects.
Y2O3 dispersoids intercept and trap radiation-induced defects.
Defect interception and recombination reduce the accumulation of dislocation loops and voids.
Reducing void and dislocation-loop density mitigates irradiation-induced swelling.
Reducing irradiation-damage density mitigates irradiation hardening.
The oxide-dispersed alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced swelling than the unmodified alloy.
The oxide-dispersed alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced hardening than the unmodified alloy.
The oxide-dispersed alloy will maintain tensile strength comparable to that of the unmodified alloy.
Under equivalent irradiation, the unmodified alloy is expected to accumulate more defects and undergo greater swelling and hardening.
The beneficial effect is expected to hold within fusion-relevant irradiation-dose and operational-temperature ranges.
Excessive oxide content or inhomogeneous oxide dispersion could eliminate the radiation-tolerance improvement or embrittle the alloy.
The defect-sink mechanism is well documented in oxide-dispersion-strengthened alloys other than the proposed refractory HEA.
